procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court in Uttar Pradesh since the case name is SANGEETA AGRAWAL & ORS. v. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR.
procedural_history.impugned_order: An order of the High Court (Single Judge) disposing of an application. The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to set out the facts of the case and examine the challenge made to the proceedings in light of the principles of law laid down by the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court (Single Judge) disposed of an application without setting out the brief facts of the case, examining the challenge made to the proceedings in light of the principles of law laid down by the Supreme Court, and recording findings with reasons to support the conclusion reached.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the case to the High Court. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to decide the appellants’ application afresh on merits in accordance with law after notice to the other side, keeping in view the observations made by the Supreme Court and after issuing notice to respondent Nos. 1 and 2.

directions: The impugned order is set aside.
The case is remanded to the High Court for its decision on merits.
The High Court shall decide the matter uninfluenced by any of our observations in this order.
The High Court shall decide the matter after notice to respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order dismissing an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for quashing proceedings is legally sustainable if it fails to set out the facts of the case, apply legal principles to those facts, and provide reasons for its conclusion.

facts: The High Court dismissed an application filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which sought to quash criminal proceedings under Sections 498A and 304B of the IPC.
Upon review, the Supreme Court found that the High Court's order only quoted general principles of law laid down in various decisions.

The High Court's order failed to mention the specific facts of the case, such as the nature of the complaint, the allegations made, the grounds on which the proceedings were challenged, and why those grounds were not sufficient for interference.
law: A court, when deciding a case, must first set out the brief facts to understand the factual matrix.
It must then examine the challenge to the proceedings in light of established legal principles.
Finally, it must record its findings with specific reasons to support its conclusion.
Providing reasons is essential as it enables a higher court to examine whether the lower court's decision is factually and legally sustainable.
application: The Supreme Court applied the legal requirement for a reasoned order to the High Court's judgment.
It found that the High Court had not performed this essential exercise.
The High Court's order lacked any discussion of the case's facts and did not apply the quoted legal principles to those facts to arrive at a reasoned conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the High Court's order failed to set out the facts, apply the law to those facts, and provide reasons for its decision, it was not legally sustainable. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remanded the matter back to the High Court for a fresh decision on the merits in accordance with the law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order dismissing an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for quashing proceedings is legally sustainable if it fails to set out the facts of the case, apply legal principles to those facts, and provide reasons for its conclusion.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's order is unsustainable because it failed to set out the factual matrix of the case, such as the nature of the complaint, the allegations, and the grounds on which the proceedings were challenged.
The High Court merely quoted legal principles laid down in several decisions without applying them to the specific facts of the case.
The order lacks any reasoning to support its conclusion, making it impossible for a higher court to examine whether the decision was factually and legally sustainable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Every judicial order must, at a minimum, set out the brief facts of the case, examine the legal challenges presented, and record the basis and reasons for its conclusion. This is required to support the conclusion reached and to enable a higher court to examine whether the reasoning is factually and legally sustainable.
obiter: Having formed an opinion to remand the case in the light of our reasoning, we do not consider it proper to go into the merits of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A High Court order disposing of an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is legally unsustainable if it fails to follow the required judicial process. The court must first set out the brief facts to understand the case's factual matrix, then examine the challenge to the proceedings in light of established legal principles, and finally, record its findings with the basis and reasons for its conclusion on whether interference is warranted. The failure to perform this exercise necessitates setting aside the order.
legal_tests_applied: For a judicial order to be sustainable, it must: (1) set out the brief facts of the case to understand the factual matrix; (2) examine the challenge made to the proceedings in light of the principles of law; and (3) record a finding as to the basis and reasons a case is made out for interference or not.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's order failed to set out the factual matrix of the case, such as the nature of the complaint, the allegations, who filed it, and the grounds on which the proceedings were challenged.
The High Court merely quoted the principles of law laid down in several decisions without applying them to the specific facts of the case to determine if a case for interference was made out.

The absence of factual context and reasoned application of law made it impossible for the Supreme Court to know the factual matrix of the case, much less to appreciate the controversy or examine the sustainability of the High Court's conclusion.
policy_considerations: Providing reasons in a judicial order is essential because it enables a higher court to examine whether the reasoning given by the court below is factually and legally sustainable.
